parole.testo: Most likely from Late Latin aprīcāre (compare the form abriar and Occitan abrigar), from Latin aprīcārī, from aprīcus. Compare Spanish abrigar, English apricate, and French abrier. Alternatively, and less likely, from Late Latin *abrigāre (“to cover, shelter”), from a- + brigare, from Frankish *birī
Maybe from Arabic المَزْرَعَة (al-mazraʕa, “farm”), or from Arabic المَشْجَرَة (al-mašjara, “woodland”).

parole.significato: to put out; to extinguish (to stop something from burning)
parole.testo: From a- + pagar, or possibly from a Vulgar Latin *appācāre, from Latin ad- + pācāre.
From a derivative of pondre (past participle post), or from a Vulgar Latin *appositāre, from Latin appositus.

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; perhaps; or from; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: Uncertain. Perhaps from Italian straccare or from Arabic تَرَقَّى (taraqqā, “to advance”).
Borrowed from French badiane, either from Persian بادیان (“fennel”) or possibly from Chinese 八角 (bājiǎo).

From bany + -ar, or from Vulgar Latin *baneare, from Late Latin balneāre, from Latin balneum. Compare Aragonese banyar, Occitan banhar, French baigner, Spanish bañar, Italian bagnare, Portuguese banhar.

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; Probably; either; modificatore <unc> nel legame; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: Uncertain. Probably either a diminutive of barra (“bar”), from Vulgar Latin *barra (“bar”), or a diminutive of Vulgar Latin *barrum (“clay, mud”), probably ultimately from Celtiberian or Paleo-Hispanic.

Unknown. From Vulgar Latin *brasa, perhaps from a pre-latin substrate or from Proto-West Germanic *brasa, from a Proto-Germanic root related to *brewwaną (“to boil, seethe, brew”). However, compare Proto-Indo-European *bʰres- (“to crack, break, burst”).

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cascunum or *casquunum, a conflation of Latin quisque ūnum (“each one”) and *catunum, from cata (<Ancient Greek κατά (katá)) ūnum. Or from a crossing of cada and Old Catalan quiscun. Compare Occitan cadun, cascun~chascun, French chacun, Italian ciascuno.

Uncertain. Possibly from *caracōlus, via metathesis, dissimilation, and change of stress of Vulgar Latin *cochleār, Latin cochlea (“snail”), from Ancient Greek κοχλίας (kokhlías, “spiral, snail shell”). Cognate with Spanish and Portuguese caracol (“snail”). Compare with cullera (“spoon”). Alternativ
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *clappa, from *clappare, from an onomatopoeic root klapp- or from a Germanic root *klappijan, compare English clap.
Perhaps from Vulgar Latin *clocila, from earlier Latin cochlea (“clam”), or from clotxa (“carapace”) + -ina.

Possibly from a Vulgar Latin *conquīsītāre (compare Occitan conquistar, Portuguese and Spanish conquistar, Italian conquistare), from Latin conquīsītus, perfect passive participle of conquīrō. It may alternatively be an old derivative of conquist, from a variant of Old Catalan conquest, the archaic
From creure + -ença or from Late Latin crēdentia (compare Occitan cresença, French croyance), from Latin crēdēns.

parole.significato: die (polyhedron with symbols on each side)
parole.testo: From a Vulgar Latin *dadu, of uncertain origin; perhaps of Arabic origin, cf. أَعْدَاد (ʔaʕdād), or alternatively from Latin datum, from datus (“given”), the past participle of dare (“to give”), from Proto-Indo-European *deh₃- (“to lay out, to spread out”). Compare French dé, Italian, Spanish, and P

parole.significato: to leave (to refrain from taking (something) away)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Catalan leixar, from Latin laxāre (compare Occitan daissar and laissar, Portuguese deixar, Aragonese deixar, Spanish dejar, French laisser and Italian lasciare). The alteration of the initial l- to d- (found in Ibero- and Occitano-Romance) may be due to the preposition de precedin

From des- + lligar, or from Vulgar Latin disligāre (attested in the Reichenau Glossary), from Latin dis- + ligō (“tie, bind”). Compare Occitan desligar, French délier, Portuguese desligar, Spanish desliar, Friulian disleâ, Italian slegare, Romanian dezlega.

Alteration of Old Catalan desparar (possibly by influence of Spanish disparar), either from des- + parar or inherited from Latin disparāre (“separate”), from dis- + parō (“make equal”), although it was taken as the negative of parō (“prepare, arrange”) in Romance.

parole.significato: to double (make twice as much or twice as large)
parole.testo: Either from doble + -ar or Late Latin duplāre, from Latin duplus.
From dreçar (cf. adreçar), or possibly a Vulgar Latin *d(ē)rēctiāria, from Latin dīrēctus.
From en- + boca + -ar, or possibly corresponding to a Vulgar Latin *imbuccāre, from Latin bucca.

Borrowed from Old Occitan empaitar, empachar, from Vulgar Latin *impāctāre, from impāctum, perfect passive participle of Latin impingō (“to drive, force”). Alternatively, from Latin impedicāre (“to fetter, entangle”), in which case it is a doublet of empatxar.
Substantivation and alteration of the Old Catalan endret (“in front of”), itself from en + dret, or possibly from Latin in directum. Compare Occitan endrech, French endroit.
From gola or from Vulgar Latin *ingullīre, a verb based on Latin gula (“throat”).
From sord or from en- + Vulgar Latin *surdīre, with conjugation from Latin surdēscere, from surdus (“deaf”) + -ēscō. Compare Spanish ensordecer, Portuguese ensurdecer, French assourdir.

parole.significato: amuse-bouche (dish with assorted meats, cheeses and other small accompaniments, served before the main course)
parole.testo: Either from Latin intermissus, perfect participle of intermittō, or from French entremets, with the same ultimate origin.
From en- + verd + -ir, or from a Vulgar Latin *invir(i)dire, from *invir(i)descere, from Latin viridēscere. Compare Spanish enverdecer, Italian inverdire, Romanian înverzi.

From envolt, past participle of Old Catalan envoldre (corresponding to Latin involūtus, perfect passive participle of involvō, involvere), or possibly from a Vulgar Latin *involtāre, for Latin involūtāre, frequentative of involvere. First attested in the 14th century. Compare Occitan envoltar, Itali
Inherited from Old Catalan escarnir, from Late Latin *scarnīre, from Proto-West Germanic *skirnijan, which could be from *skeran (“to shear”), or possibly related to *skarn (“dung, filth”).

From es- + collir, or possibly from a Vulgar Latin *excolligere, from Latin ex- + colligere (“to gather”). Compare Galician escoller, Spanish escoger, Portuguese escolher, Asturian escoyer, Extremaduran escogel.

Deverbal from escombrar, from Vulgar Latin *excomborāre, from Proto-Celtic *comboros, derived from *kom- (“with”) + *bereti (“to bear”), or from Latin scōpa, crossed with the Celtic word or influenced by escombrar (compare Occitan escoba, Aragonese escoba and the Ibero-Romance variants).
Borrowed from Old French escote, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *skautaz, either via Frankish *skōta or Old Norse skaut.
From escut + -er or from Late Latin scūtārius, from Latin scūtum (“shield”).
From espia + -ar, or from Vulgar Latin *spiāre, from Gothic or Frankish *spehōn, from Proto-Germanic *spehōną (“to see, look”), from Proto-Indo-European *speḱ- (“to look”).
Uncertain; possibly pre-Roman, from an Proto-Indo-European root *pur- (“fire”). Also found in Old Catalan and Aragonese as purna. Alternatively, linked to Latin prūna (“burning coal”).
Possibly from a Late Latin *stancāre, derived by metathesis from stagnō, or from a Vulgar Latin *stanticāre, from stāns (“standing”).

parole.significato: to horseshoe, to shoe a horse
parole.testo: From ferro (“iron”) + -ar, or from a Late Latin ferrāre, from Latin ferrum (“iron”). Compare Occitan ferrar, French ferrer, Portuguese ferrar, Spanish herrar, Italian ferrare.
From foc + -era, or from Late Latin, Vulgar Latin *focāria, from Latin focārius (“of a hearth”), from focus (“(controlled) fire”). Compare Spanish hoguera, Portuguese fogueira.
Inherited from Old Catalan foure, from Proto-Germanic *fōdrą (“sheath”) either via Frankish *fōdr or Gothic 𐍆𐍉𐌳𐍂 (fōdr).
From Latin fungus, or possibly a calque of Spanish hongo.
Either from an earlier *fornau, from Latin fornax (“furnace”), or from Vulgar Latin *furnale, from furnus (“oven”).

parole.significato: hinge (device that allows the pivoting of a door)
parole.testo: From earlier frantissa, either via Old Catalan frant, past participle of frànyer (“to break”), or directly from a Vulgar Latin *fractītia. Either way, ultimately from Latin frangō and modified by folk etymology due to being associated with front.

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; Possibly; Probably; or from; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: Uncertain. Probably from a substrate language. Maybe related with Proto-Brythonic *gwɨmon, from Proto-Celtic *wimmonā, and this possibly from a non-IE substrate language or from Proto-Indo-European *weyb- (“to wind around”). Cognate with Portuguese gamão, Spanish gamón and Galician gamón.

parole.significato: crop (part of the alimentary track of birds)
parole.testo: Attested since the 13th century, with the origin being in the regions of Valencia and the Balearic Islands. Due to this, a Mozarabic origin has been proposed. Alternatively, borrowed from Occitan gavach. If of Mozarabic origin, it would come from a Vulgar Latin base *gauaktio-, if borrowed from Occi
Either inherited from Latin genium or a clipping of enginy, from Latin ingenium.
From the verb governar, or possibly from Late Latin gubernus or gubernius, from Latin gubernum or gubernō.
First attested in 1905. Borrowed either from French impôt, or directly from Latin impositus.
Substantivation and alteration of the Old Catalan endret (“in front of”), itself from en + dret, or possibly from Latin in directum. Compare Occitan endrech, French endroit.
From Vulgar Latin *jolium viride (“green darnel”), from lolium, or possibly from Latin līlium viride (“green lily”). Compare Occitan jolverd.
Deverbal from llampar, from Late Latin lampāre; alternatively perhaps from a Vulgar Latin *lampu (compare Occitan lamp, Italian lampo), from Latin lampas.

Most likely from Vulgar Latin *lapāre, lappāre, from Frankish *lapan (“to lick up, lap”). Compare Occitan lepar (“to lick”), French laper (“to lap”), Dutch leppen (“to lap”), Icelandic lepja (“to lap”). Alternatively, from a Vulgar Latin root *lippare or *lippicare, from lippus or lippio, cf. Liguri

Uncertain. Perhaps from a Vulgar Latin *lextus or *lestus, reduced from *lexitus, as an alteration of Latin lēctus (“chosen; read”), participle of legō. Alternatively of Germanic origin, possibly from Proto-Germanic *listiz. Compare Spanish listo, Portuguese and Italian lesto.
Probably borrowed from Spanish lóbrego, from either Latin lubricus (“slippery”) or by metathesis from Latin lūgubris (“gloomy”).
Borrowed from French manivelle, which ultimately derives either from Latin manicula or manuālis.
Inherited from Old Catalan mant. Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *managiþō, cognate with Old French maint, or possibly from a conflation of tantus (“many”) + magnum (“large”).
Borrowed from French manivelle, which ultimately derives either from Latin manicula or manuālis.
Borrowed from Latin smaragdus, or from Ancient Greek σμάραγδος (smáragdos), of Semitic origin.
From marca + -ar or from Vulgar Latin *marcāre, of Germanic origin.

Inherited from Old Catalan martell, from Late Latin martellus, itself a diminutive of martulus, variant of Latin marculus, or alternatively based on malleus. Compare Occitan martèl, French marteau, Portuguese martelo and Italian martello.
Most likely from Latin mactāre (through a Vulgar Latin root *mattāre). Alternatively, possibly from Vulgar Latin *mattāre, from Late Latin mattus (“drunk, intoxicated”), related to madidus.
Either from Vulgar Latin *merciārius or from Old Catalan merç (“commodity”), both ultimately from Latin merx (“merchandise, goods”).

Possibly a deverbal of nusar, from Vulgar Latin *nōdāre, from Latin nōdus. Alternatively, from the plural of nu, from older Old Catalan nuu, from Vulgar Latin *nūdus, alteration of Latin nōdus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gned-, *gnod- (“to bind”). Compare Occitan nos, French nœud, Spanish
From núvol + -ós, or from Late Latin nūbilōsus, ultimately from Latin nūbēs (“cloud”). Compare Occitan nivolós.

From Italian oricello, from Latin ōricilla, diminutive of ōricula (variant of auricula), both diminutives of auris (“ear”)) + illa (a double diminutive suffix) or from auris (“ear”) + cula + illa, influenced by dialectal Arabic [script needed] ('urjālla).

Inherited from Old Catalan palissa (“fence, palisade”) (especially in the context of jousting), either borrowed from Spanish paliza or an indigenous formation, in either case etymologically Latin pālus (“stake”) and perhaps -icea. The change from /l/ to /ʎ/ is likely by analogy with lliça or vall.
Borrowed from French piller. The sense of "grab" is from Italian pigliare, either via direct borrowing or through the mediation of Spanish pillar.
From the feminine of plat, or from Vulgar Latin *platta, *plattus, borrowed from Ancient Greek πλατύς (platús, “wide”), because silver was often made into sheets.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin pullicella, of disputed origin. Possibly a diminutive of Latin pullus (“young of animals, chick”). Alternatively from Latin puella (“girl”) through a Vulgar Latin root *puellicella. Cognate with French pucelle.
From porta + -er or from Old Catalan porter, from Late Latin portārius, from Latin porta. Compare French portier.

Ultimately from Latin pungō (“to puncture”), either analogically derived from Catalan punxí, from the perfect form of the Latin verb, or through a Vulgar Latin *punctiāre, itself possibly reaching Catalan (and the Spanish equivalent punchar) through a Valencian Mozarabic intermediate. Compare also S
Inherited from Old Catalan quet, dialectal variant of quiet, or from Vulgar Latin *quētāre, from Late Latin quiētāre, from Latin quiētārī. See also quitar.

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; Possibly; or from; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: Uncertain. Possibly from Proto-Basque *karri (“rock”) (compare Basque harri), or from Proto-Celtic *karr- (“rock”) (compare Welsh craig, Irish creag, Manx creg, Armenian քար (kʻar)).

Borrowed from Arabic اَلْكِيمِيَاء (al-kīmiyāʔ), from Ancient Greek χυμείᾱ (khumeíā), or from Latin chimicus, alternative form of chēmicus (“chemical”), from chēmia (“chemistry”), Ancient Greek χυμείᾱ (khumeíā, “art of alloying metals”), from χύμα (khúma, “fluid”).

From a derivative of Latin rāpum (“turnip”), developing a sense of "tail" in many Romance languages of Iberia, such as Spanish, Portuguese, and Galician rabo. Alternatively, possibly from Old Spanish rabosa, itself of the same origin.
From a mix of recaptar and regatar with the prefix res- instead, or from Vulgar Latin *reexcaptāre, from Latin captāre. Compare Spanish rescatar.
Either a derivative of ruïna, or from a related Vulgar Latin root *ruinīnus, reduced through haplology to *ruīnus, ultimately from Latin ruīna. Compare Spanish ruin, Portuguese ruim.

Of unknown origin. Possibly from Tatar чабата (çabata, “overshoes”), ultimately either from Ottoman Turkish چاپوت (çaput, çapıt, “patchwork, tatters”), from Ottoman Turkish چاپمق (çapmak, “to slap on”), or of Iranian origin, cognate with modern Persian چپت (čapat, “a kind of traditional leather shoe

parole.significato: to leave, to get out from, to gush
parole.testo: From Latin salīre or from Occitan salhir.
From terra, or possibly a Late Latin subterrō, subterrāre, from Latin sub + terra. Compare also Occitan sosterrar.
From tes (“tight”), or possibly from a Vulgar Latin *tēnsāre, from Latin tēnsus, perfect passive participle of tendō.
From teula (“tile”), from Vulgar Latin *tegla, from Latin tēgula, or from a root *teglāta, from tēgulātum, from tēgula. Compare Spanish tejado, Portuguese telhado, Galician tellado.

Ultimately from Vulgar Latin *thymellus, diminutive of Latin thymus, from Ancient Greek θύμος (thúmos). Borrowed into Catalan either from Spanish tomillo, with some kind of vowel adaptation, or more likely from Valencian Mozarabic.

Borrowed from Middle High German trampen (“to walk heavily”), or from Medieval Latin trappa, from Proto-Germanic *trap-, from Proto-Indo-European *dremb- (“to run”); or possibly ultimately onomatopoeic.

Inherited from Old Catalan trencar, itself possibly from a Vulgar Latin *trinicāre (“cut into three parts”), from the root trini, based on duplicāre, or alternatively from an alteration of Latin truncāre. It may also derive from or be influenced by a pre-Roman, possibly Gaulish word, cf. *trincare (

Uncertain. Most likely from Vulgar Latin *traucem, from Latin trāducem, accusative of trādux (“vine branch”). Alternatively, from Latin thyrsus, from Ancient Greek θύρσος (thúrsos). Cognates include Aragonese troz, Spanish trozo and probably Italian tozzo.

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; alternatively; or possibly
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Catalan truja, from Late Latin troia, of uncertain origin, but possibly * from Latin (porcum de) Troia (“(hog of) Troy”), after the Trojan horse, * or alternatively of Celtic origin, from a Gaulish root *trogja, from a root meaning “to pull” and thence also “fertile," Proto-Celtic
Borrowed from Middle French turbant or from Italian turbante, both ultimately from Persian دلبند (dolband).
Inherited from Latin vocāre (“call”), or alternatively from a Proto-Germanic *wagōną (“to sway, fluctuate”), or related to French voguer. Compare also Spanish bogar, Italian vogare.
Inherited from Old Catalan voltor, from Latin vulturius, or possibly through a Vulgar Latin *vultōrem. Compare Occitan voltor; French vautour; Italian avvoltoio, avvoltore.
Probably from Vulgar Latin *sūctulāre, from Latin sūctus, from sūgō. Alternatively, of onomatopoeic origin. Compare Spanish chupar.
